The Abu mullet (Planiliza abu), a freshwater mugilid endemic to the river systems of the Middle East, exhibits life-history traits typical of a fast-growing, relatively short-lived fish. Field surveys conducted in the Shatt al-Arab basin indicate that the species attains a maximum total length of 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters], a modest size compared to its more marine congeners. This ultimate length is reached through a period of rapid somatic growth during the first two years of life, after which growth decelerates markedly. Individuals collected during mark-recapture studies have been documented to achieve a maximum lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years] at a water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C] under natural conditions, a duration that aligns with the general pattern observed in other small-bodied, iteroparous cypriniforms inhabiting warm, productive lowland rivers. The relatively high metabolic demand imposed by the warm, thermally stable waters of its habitat likely drives this abbreviated longevity, as somatic maintenance costs at sustained high temperatures typically accelerate the aging process in teleosts.

Reproductive maturation in Planiliza abu occurs at a body size substantially smaller than the ultimate length, with the onset of puberty characterized by the first visible gonadal development. Studies examining the gonadosomatic index of wild-caught specimens have established that sexual maturity is attained at a total length of 12.4 centimeters [Lp = 12.4 centimeters], corresponding to a point when individuals have completed just over sixty percent of their asymptotic growth. At this pubertal length, the corresponding body mass of the fish is approximately 15.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 15.6 grams], based on length-weight regressions derived from a large sample collected across multiple seasons. This mass at puberty represents a critical threshold for the allocation of energetic resources away from continued somatic investment and toward the production of gametes, a shift that is particularly pronounced in females, who must channel substantial energy into vitellogenesis and oocyte maturation.

For female Abu mullet that have completed their growth, the maximum recorded adult body mass is 63.4 grams [Wwi = 63.4 grams], reflecting the energetic ceiling imposed by the relationship between length and mass at the asymptotic size. This ultimate wet weight for females is a key determinant of fecundity, as larger females are capable of carrying more advanced oocytes. The reproductive strategy of this species involves intermittent batch spawning over an extended breeding season, a pattern that allows females to maximize lifetime fecundity despite the constraints of a finite body size. At the other end of the life cycle, the egg itself is notably small, with the estimated initial wet weight of the fertilized ovum calculated at 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], a value derived from the geometric relationship of a spherical egg of 0.7 millimeters in diameter. This minute egg mass places the species firmly within the pelagic-spawning guild, where numerous small eggs are released into the water column rather than a few large, yolky ones.

The reproductive output of Planiliza abu is tightly coupled to water temperature, with peak spawning activity observed when the thermal regime reaches a specific threshold. Under experimental conditions maintained at a constant 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], gravid females have been observed to release eggs at a rate corresponding to a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 155 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 155 eggs per day], which translates to a total annual fecundity of about 56,400 eggs per year. This substantial annual reproductive output helps compensate for the high rates of egg and larval mortality typical of pelagic spawners in turbid freshwater environments. The 27.3 °C temperature represents an optimal thermal window for both gametogenesis and the successful development of the yolk-sac larvae, as it balances the enzymatic kinetics of yolk absorption with the metabolic cost incurred by the developing embryo.

The longevity of Planiliza abu is further contextualized by the thermal conditions of its natural habitat. In the warm, shallow waters of its native range, the species completes its entire life cycle from fertilized egg to natural death at a temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C] within approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years]. This lifespan, while modest in absolute terms, is consistent with the predictions of metabolic theory for a fish of its size living in a high-temperature environment. The interplay between the maximum total length of 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters] and the lifespan underscores a fundamental life-history trade-off: the rapid growth needed to reach reproductive size quickly comes at the cost of a shorter overall life expectancy. Comparative data from other mugilid species in the region suggest that the relatively low size at puberty of 12.4 centimeters [Lp = 12.4 centimeters] is an adaptation to early maturation in an unpredictable hydrological environment, ensuring that at least some individuals reproduce before seasonal floods or droughts can disrupt the spawning season.
